accuracy.reason: Nine objectives correctly distinguish replicated copies/shards, snapshot-log handoff, async and configured sync acknowledgment, receipt/durability/application, lag/routing, leader arrangements, safe failover, retained history and requirement-driven policy. Live PostgreSQL, RDS, MySQL, Cassandra and Brewer passages support the limits.

evidence.quote: Adding read replicas can increase read capacity. It does not automatically increase the number of writes the system can handle.

mechanisms.reason: The stack traces snapshot plus ordered changes, acknowledgment before propagation, unapplied replica reads and candidate/fencing/routing takeover. Diagrams preserve receive/apply separation, lagging profile and fencing-before-promotion example. Historical recovery uses backup plus retained logs, not a current-copy promise.

evidence.quote: Start with an initial copy, then receive and apply later changes.

coherence.reason: Given server/database/network prerequisites suffice; copy mechanics precede acknowledgment, lag, topology, failover and backup decisions. All card prerequisites and distinctions are taught; learner integrates the full chain.

evidence.quote: The trade-off is less waiting during writes, in exchange for older reads and possible loss of recent writes during failover.

decisions.reason: Every guarantee is traded against waiting, replica dependency, load, stale reads, loss windows or operating cost. Final policy explicitly asks tolerated loss/freshness/downtime before replica-count choices; no zero-loss or unlimited-write guarantee.

evidence.quote: Synchronous replication does not necessarily wait for every replica. Nor does every synchronous mode guarantee that replica reads already show the change.

clarity.reason: Technical terms are defined and the receive/store/apply distinction is concrete. Diagram captions align with actual state; shared renderer/CSS inspected only. Learner gaps are implementation-specific algorithms/targets outside the foundational objectives.

evidence.quote: A fixed sleep or low average lag is not proof that a particular write is visible.

outcomes.reason: Criteria 1-6 satisfied: learner defines copies versus shards, eligible read/recovery purpose and limits, snapshot/log ordered continuation, aligned starting position and receiving versus applying; slides 1-2 support it.

Criteria 1-7 satisfied: learner traces acknowledged async write loss, latency benefit, configured sync replica count/stage, receipt/durable/apply differences and waiting/failure trade-offs without all-copy or all-failure guarantees; slides 3-4 support it.

Criteria 1-8 satisfied: learner explains lag stage and read-your-writes, authoritative-primary versus specific-applied-write wait versus stale-tolerant routing, load/failover limits, and single/multi/leaderless writes with conflict/repair duties; slides 5-6 support all.

Criteria 1-7 satisfied: learner distinguishes silence from death, suitable progress-qualified promotion, fencing/split brain, client redirection, lost async writes, propagated deletes, retained backup/log history and measured usable restore. Slide 7-8 and earlier acknowledgment support; no exact eligibility algorithm is required.

Criteria 1-4 satisfied: learner first elicits loss/freshness/latency/recovery/failure targets; proposes conditional durable sync acknowledgment plus replica reports/freshness routing, safe takeover, retained backups and tested restoration with progress/health/write-wait monitoring. It correctly avoids specifying unsupported zero-loss/zero-downtime guarantees.

sourceChecks.claim: Live RDS read-replica introduction confirms read-only copies and query routing reduce primary read load; no automatic write scale or safe promotion guarantee.

Live PostgreSQL logical replication describes initial snapshot, continual later changes and same-order subscriber application; contrasts logical data-level with physical byte/block replication. Handoff alignment follows this model.
Live PostgreSQL warm standby explicitly says asynchronous committed transactions may not reach standby before primary crash and can be lost at failover.
Live synchronous replication section distinguishes configured standby count/set and remote_write/on/remote_apply, replay visibility, commit waits and performance/availability costs.

Live MySQL WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET monitors applied transactions with success/timeout/error results; this supports waiting for specific progress rather than fixed sleep. PostgreSQL apply distinction confirms received is not yet readable.

Live Cassandra Dynamo describes coordinator sending writes to replicas, configured response counts, repair and timestamp reconciliation. PostgreSQL leader replication supports single-leader ordering; independent multi-writer conflict costs are correctly bounded.

Live PostgreSQL failover requires preventing the old primary from remaining primary to avoid competing authority/data loss; replica selection/routing and silence uncertainty are necessary safety deductions.

Live PostgreSQL PITR describes backup plus archived WAL, chosen replay stopping point before accidental deletion and recovery failure/restart. Retained history and tested usable restore are properly required.

Live Brewer retrospective supports operation-dependent behavior during partitions and recovery. Earlier checked replication sources supply acknowledgment/routing/recovery costs behind the final requirements-first synthesis.
